title: Integration & Gateway SDK Discovery - MarinerOps
summary: Intro discovery covering MarinerOps' requirements for hosted vs private deployment, SDK integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits, and observability hooks. Agreed to run a small pilot using Redwood hosted with gateway proxy to validate latency and cost before exploring Private deployment.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
SDK language support and LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors
Observability hooks: traces, per-request tokens, cost metrics
Pilot plan: benchmarks and success criteria
action_items: Maya Chen - Send pricing deck and Hosted pilot contract template - due 2028-06-09
Rafael Ortiz - Share SDK examples for LangChain and a sample LlamaIndex connector repo - due 2028-06-10
Victor Kim - Provide current traffic shape and peak RPS numbers, plus sample prompt complexity - due 2028-06-09
next_steps: Schedule 60m pilot kickoff next week (hosted evaluation)
Redwood to provide sandbox API key and a small benchmarking script
Customer to run 48h smoke test and report latency/99th percentiles
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-06-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Leah Park (CTO - MarinerOps), Victor Kim (Staff Engineer), Anya Singh (Product)

Summary: quick discovery to map MarinerOps' integration needs — SDK support, connectors with LangChain/LlamaIndex, where to put a gateway/proxy (edge vs in-VPC), rate-limiting shaping, and what observability hooks they need to ship safely.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, this is Maya from Redwood, i'm joined by Rafael our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Leah Park: good thanks, busy but excited to talk through this.
[00:12] Rafael Ortiz: hi all, quick intro from me — i focus on infra and integrations, happy to dig into SDKs, proxies, and perf.
[00:19] Victor Kim: perfect, i'll run the technical questions. Anya will cover product/metrics.
[00:24] Anya Singh: yeah thanks, short on time so we'll try to be concise.
[00:29] Maya Chen: great, high level — MarinerOps is evaluating Redwood for customer-facing generative features, right? can you paint the 30k-foot picture and the success criteria?
[00:38] Leah Park: sure — we're building a recommendations + natural language assistant in our merchant dashboard. need sub-300ms p50 for short prompts, p95 around 750ms ideally, and cost per 1k tokens can't blow up our margins. security and audit logs are non-negotiable — SOC2-ish controls, KMS for key management, and ability to run in our VPC eventually.
[01:05] Maya Chen: thank you. two quick clarifying q's: are you leaning hosted first or going to private on day one? and do you plan to use LangChain/LlamaIndex or direct SDKs?
[01:18] Leah Park: hosted first to move fast — pilot in next 2 weeks. we'll likely prototype with LangChain internally, but final product uses our in-house orchestration so we might need a LlamaIndex connector for some retrieval flows.
[01:31] Rafael Ortiz: makes sense. for hosted pilots we typically provide a sandbox API key and a small client lib. our SDKs support Python, Node, and a psuedo-TS/Go wrapper. we also maintain LangChain examples and a LlamaIndex adapter.
[01:46] Victor Kim: is the LlamaIndex adapter maintained by Redwood or community?
[01:49] Rafael Ortiz: we have an official adapter repo — it's lightweight, you can plug in your docstores and it handles the retrieval calls and batching for the backend. we'll share sample code.
[01:58] Anya Singh: on auth — we need single sign-on for ops and role-based access for which team can deploy models. how are enterprise roles handled?
[02:06] Maya Chen: for enterprise customers we support SSO via SAML/Okta and granular RBAC in the Console. for Private deployments RBAC integrates with your IdP. audit logs are available — both API-level and token-level traces.
[02:18] Leah Park: great. now the tricky part: network topology. we have a gateway service today that proxies requests through our edge, does rate limit, and attaches merchant metadata. we want to keep that but might consider using Redwood's gateway/proxy for token billing and observability. what's recommended?
[02:35] Rafael Ortiz: quick sketch — two common patterns: 1) Place Redwood as an upstream model endpoint behind your existing gateway (you keep auth and metadata enrichment), or 2) deploy a lightweight Redwood proxy in your VPC that does tokenized routing and sends telemetry back to Redwood's control plane. Option 1 is easiest for hosted; Option 2 is common for Private/VPC to avoid egress and keep data in-network.
[02:58] Victor Kim: in Option 1, do we have to send customer PII to Redwood? we're sensitive about passing raw user messages off-network.
[03:07] Rafael Ortiz: hosted means content leaves your network to Redwood's hosted runtime — you can opt into request redaction and we offer in-flight encryption and retention policies. for sensitive data customers prefer Private with a VPC peering or on-prem package.
[03:21] Leah Park: got it. we can start hosted with redaction for pilot. next — rate limits. our spike traffic sometimes bursts to 600 RPS for short windows. can Redwood handle that with the hosted plan? and how are quotas applied per-token vs per-request?
[03:38] Maya Chen: for hosted we have tiered rate limits and burst windows; the default quota uses tokens-per-minute plus a concurrent request cap. for pilots we can temporarily raise quotas. Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput for sustained high RPS.
[03:52] Victor Kim: what's the behavior when quotas are hit — 429s or queueing? can we set up graceful degradation routes?
[03:58] Rafael Ortiz: by default you get 429s. we recommend client-side retries with exponential backoff and token-bucket smoothing. Redwood Console supports routing policies — you can set a fallback to a cheaper model variant or cached response on quota exhaustion. we can also enable automatic canary fallback to an LLM with smaller context window to preserve UX.
[04:19] Anya Singh: observability — we need per-request token breakdown, latency percentiles per model, and trace ids that join our distributed traces. how does Redwood expose that?
[04:28] Rafael Ortiz: we include tracing headers you can inject (x-redwood-trace) and we emit span events to existing back-ends via OTLP. the Console shows token-level cost per call and per-route dashboards; there's an API to pull raw events for your analytics.
[04:43] Victor Kim: OTLP — does that mean we can point to our internal Jaeger/Tempo?
[04:47] Rafael Ortiz: yes, OTLP-compatible endpoints work for Private deployments; for Hosted we push to your partner endpoints via secure webhooks or you can pull logs via our API.
[04:57] Leah Park: about SDKs again — we use LangChain chains and a LlamaIndex Retriever flow. are there built-in batching and KV cache hooks to avoid re-sending context repeatedly?
[05:07] Rafael Ortiz: yes — our SDK provides a KV cache layer and embeddings caching. LangChain integration includes a batching wrapper that aggregates similar requests into a single inference call where appropriate. KV cache is client-side but we support a unified cache sync for Private deployments to keep KV near the model.
[05:23] Victor Kim: curious about streaming — we need partial responses to the UI. does the SDK support SSE/WebSocket streaming and token-level credits?
[05:30] Rafael Ortiz: streaming via SSE or websockets is supported. we expose tokens as they are emitted and you can optionally attach provisional cost estimates in the streaming payload. the Console reconciles billed tokens after call completion.
[05:43] Anya Singh: about model rollouts — we want canary testing and A/B. does Redwood support per-route model pins and traffic splitting?
[05:51] Maya Chen: yes, Console supports pinning models per route and configuring percentage-based traffic splits. you can also set automatic rollback on quality regressions if you feed eval hooks.
[05:59] Leah Park: good. on pricing — will you send a sample for pilot pricing vs projected for Dedicated? we need to budget.
[06:04] Maya Chen: i'll send a pricing deck with hosted pilot rates, and an indicative Dedicated quote for the numbers you shared.
[06:10] Victor Kim: one more network question — if we place a proxy in our VPC, how does auth flow? do we exchange tokens?
[06:16] Rafael Ortiz: typical flow: your gateway signs requests to the VPC proxy using mTLS or signed JWTs. the proxy validates, attaches Redwood tenant headers, and forwards to the runtime or local model. For hosted flows you can also use short-lived API keys and a fronting proxy to avoid embedding long-lived keys in the client.
[06:32] Leah Park: retention and data residency — we operate in EU primary. can hosted guarantee EU-only processing and storage?
[06:38] Maya Chen: we have regional hosting options and can guarantee data residency in EU regions for hosted customers with contractual terms. Private solves it entirely if required.
[06:48] Anya Singh: for the pilot we want to validate latency and cost with our live traffic shape. what's the recommended benchmark script?
[06:55] Rafael Ortiz: we'll give a small Python loadgen that can replay request traces, parameterized by prompt length distribution and RPS. it reports p50/p95/p99 and token counts so you can calculate projected costs.
[07:06] Victor Kim: can we simulate caching benefits — e.g., prefix caching for repeated prompts?
[07:10] Rafael Ortiz: yes, the loadgen supports a cache-hit ratio parameter to simulate prefix/KV cache. we'll also enable the prefix caching feature in the sandbox for you to test.
[07:19] Maya Chen: switching gears — any blockers from your side to run the pilot?
[07:22] Leah Park: internal security review needs a SOC2 summary, KMS integration docs, and network topology options. if we see that, we can sign the pilot paperwork.
[07:33] Maya Chen: we'll attach our security pack and a one-page pilot SLA.
[07:36] Anya Singh: on instrumentation — we need per-customer usage breakdown, not just per-route; our billing ties back to merchant IDs.
[07:44] Rafael Ortiz: we can accept metadata headers (merchant-id) and break down cost per-merchant in the Console. for high-volume customers, we recommend passing an id in the signature so we can attribute tokens accurately.
[07:56] Victor Kim: about SDK languages — do you provide a first-class Go SDK, or is Go community-supported?
[08:01] Rafael Ortiz: first-class for Python and Node; Go and Java are community SDKs maintained by Redwood with enterprise support available. for performance-sensitive flows we usually recommend calling the HTTP API directly from Go with our signed header pattern.
[08:13] Leah Park: okay. time check — about 30min in. Rafael, can you quickly show the folder layout of the LangChain examples and what's in the LlamaIndex adapter?
[08:21] Rafael Ortiz: sure — (screen share implied) in the repo we have /examples/langchain/python, /examples/llamaindex with a retriever class, a small docker-compose to run a local vector store, and a benchmarks folder. the adapter handles chunking, embedding calls, and retrieval batching; minimal glue code.
[08:40] Victor Kim: any special kernel/quantization notes for latency? we want small models for latency-sensitive paths and larger ones for quality.
[08:47] Rafael Ortiz: we ship quantized variants and have runtime kernel selection based on sequence length. for short prompts we pick a quantized 4-bit variant which is much faster; for long context we use a full-precision variant. Dedicated deployments let you pin specific model builds.
[09:03] Anya Singh: back to routing — can Redwood's Console do conditional routing by header values? e.g., route merchant-tier=enterprise to Dedicated and others to Hosted.
[09:12] Maya Chen: yes, routing policies can match headers and route to different model pools, regions, or fallback rules.
[09:18] Leah Park: what about billing visibility — we need a daily charge estimate and token breakdown to integrate into our internal billing system.
[09:25] Rafael Ortiz: we provide a cost-analytics API and webhook for usage events. you can pull per-tenant token counts hourly or receive batched daily summaries.
[09:34] Victor Kim: a few nitty-gritty questions: 1) How do you count streaming tokens? 2) Are embeddings billed differently? 3) Do cache hits reduce billed tokens?
[09:44] Rafael Ortiz: streaming tokens are billed on generated/consumed tokens as reconciled at call end. embeddings are billed per-embedding vector generated. cache hits are usually free if served from the client's cache; if Redwood's runtime serves from its cache we bill the inference that produced the vector originally, subsequent reads can be billed at a lower retrieval rate depending on your plan — we can clarify exact billing in the pricing deck.
[10:04] Maya Chen: we are about halfway through — any other must-haves?
[10:08] Leah Park: SSO, KMS, EU data residency on the list. plus a short forensic log for queries flagged by our content filters.
[10:18] Rafael Ortiz: we have a flagged-queries export that includes anonymized payloads and token breakdowns for flagged items; for Private we can expose raw logs into your SIEM.
[10:28] Anya Singh: we'd like an SLA for p95 latency for Dedicated; is that standard?
[10:33] Maya Chen: SLA targets are part of Dedicated contracts — we can include a p95 target with financials. for Hosted we publish typical p95s by model in our catalog but the SLA is weaker.
[10:44] Victor Kim: technical deep dive question: when you do continuous batching, how do you maintain low tail latency? do you have early cutoffs?
[10:52] Rafael Ortiz: yes — runtime uses smart batching with per-request latency SLOs. it will cut a batch if a high-priority low-latency request enters and will route to a lower-batched path for strict SLOs. there's also KV cache hits which avoid the full model path.
[11:07] Leah Park: ok that makes sense. on the pilot, what's the minimum dataset or traffic we need to get meaningful numbers?
[11:12] Rafael Ortiz: 48 hours of production-like traffic with peak bursts simulated and a few thousand unique merchant contexts will give you stable p95/p99 numbers.
[11:22] Maya Chen: wrapping toward next steps: we'll share the security docs and the sandbox API key. Rafael will send the SDK examples and the benchmarking script. you'll run the 48h smoke test and we'll reconvene at the pilot kickoff.
[11:35] Victor Kim: timeline — can we start the sandbox on Monday?
[11:38] Maya Chen: yes, sandbox keys and initial quota by Monday EOD.
[11:42] Anya Singh: we'll aim to complete the smoke test by Friday.
[11:45] Leah Park: any concerns about token leakage through logs? our legal team worries about retention in hosted.
[11:51] Rafael Ortiz: we'll show the redact-at-source options and confirm retention windows; for legal you can request a zero-retention sandbox.
[11:59] Maya Chen: perfect. final quick recap and owners?
[12:03] Leah Park: recap — Redwood to provide security pack and sandbox, customer to run 48h test, Redwood to provide cost/benchmark script.
[12:12] Victor Kim: owners as per action items earlier.
[12:15] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.
[12:18] Meeting end.
